Every hand-written JSON call in `Sources/` — 52 sites, 31 files, five targets — now goes through one facade that names the rule it applies. Design and reasoning: `docs/adr/0004-one-json-codec.md` (first commit).

> Based on #83; the diff here is only the JSON work. Retargets to `main` once that merges.

## Why

Thirty of those files called a bare `JSONDecoder()`. **Exactly one place configured anything** — `JSONDecoder.reachyDaemon`, which knows FastAPI emits ISO 8601 with fractional seconds and that the same field sometimes arrives without them. Four sites used it; everything else took the defaults, whether it was reading the robot's answer or its own file. So the rule existed and was half-applied, and nothing said out loud that the records on disk were written with the defaults and cannot survive a change of them.

## Three profiles, and one of them is a wire format

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `.daemon` | the robot said it | ISO 8601, with or without fractional seconds |
| `.web` | Hugging Face said it | Foundation defaults, free to follow the service |
| `.stored` | **we** wrote it | Foundation defaults, **frozen** |

`.stored` is the encoding of records on users' devices right now — the catalogue in `Caches`, the widget's snapshot in the App Group, SSH and Hugging Face credentials in the Keychain. A changed strategy does not reformat them; it makes them undecodable, and every store here reports that as an empty cache rather than as an error. `StoredFormatTests` pins it at the byte level for two records, and both were confirmed to go red when the strategy is changed.

There is no default profile on purpose: a default is how thirty files took Foundation's settings without ever deciding to.

`ReachyJSON` is a leaf target on Foundation alone, for the reason `Package.swift` already gives twice — `ReachySSH` and `HuggingFaceAuth` deliberately do not depend on `ReachyKit`, so a codec living there would be shared by everything except the two targets that were pushed out of it.

## The engine stays Foundation, and that was measured

The occasion was a proposal to adopt [swift-yyjson](https://github.com/mattt/swift-yyjson). Measured in Release against this app's own payloads, it is genuinely faster — 1.3× on free-form JSON, 4.3× on concrete types — and it was still refused:

**`1.5` decodes as `1`.** `OpenAPIValueContainer` identifies a value by trying `Bool`, then `Int`, then `Double`, and relies on `Int` refusing a fractional number; that decoder rounds instead. On real data it turns `mean_control_loop_frequency: 49.58` into `49` and `max_control_loop_interval: 0.0207` into `0` — the robot's health screen reporting a zero — and a catalogue record encoded through it came out 106 KB shorter, silently. Where it is fastest we have no data, and the one megabyte-scale payload goes through the generated client, whose `Converter` builds its own `JSONDecoder` with no injection point.

`JSONCodecFreeFormTests` is the gate any future engine passes first, and it was verified to fail under mutation.

## Enforcement

A SwiftLint `custom_rules` entry refuses a bare coder under `Sources/`, proven to fire and to stay silent on the facade itself and on the two sanctioned `JSONSerialization` sites (`SetTargetClient`, `ReachyKitError`). Test fixtures are deliberately not covered — with the consequence written down: a test that decodes a daemon payload with a bare coder does not exercise the date rule.

## Verification

- 1207 tests, SwiftLint `--strict` clean, `format-check` clean, `build:app` (macOS) green.
- Behaviour-preserving, with one directional exception: sites that previously used a bare decoder now gain the daemon's date rule, which can only turn a previously-throwing decode into a successful one.
- Each of the five tasks was reviewed independently, and the whole branch again at the end; the freeze tests and the engine gate were each checked by mutation rather than by reading.
EOF

input.content:
---
name: stacked-prs-get-no-ci
description: A PR based on another branch runs zero CI jobs here, and merging to main skips the four heavy jobs
metadata:
  type: project
---

`ci.yml` triggers on `pull_request: branches: ["main"]`, so a **stacked PR** — one whose base is another
feature branch — gets **no checks at all**, silently. It only starts running once the parent merges and
GitHub retargets it to `main`.

Worse in combination: a push to `main` runs only `Lint & Test` and `Warm the SPM cache`; the four heavy
jobs (`App Build (macOS)`, `App Build (iOS + widget)`, `Smoke`, `Preview Build`) carry
`if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'` and are **skipped**. So a change that lands through a stacked PR
can reach `main` having never been built as an app anywhere — which is exactly how the widget breaks, since
`build:app:ios` is the only job that compiles it (see [[deploy-visual-fixes-to-device]]).

Observed 2026-08-12: PRs #83 and #84 were stacked; #84 never reported a check, #83's run was `cancelled` by
the merge itself, and the resulting `main` commit had no app build behind it. Ran `mise run build:app:ios`
by hand afterwards to close the gap — it passed.

**Why:** the trigger filter and the `pull_request`-only job guards are each reasonable alone and together
leave a hole a stacked PR falls straight through.

**How to apply:** don't stack PRs in this repo unless the parent merges first — or accept that the child
must be verified locally, `build:app:ios` included. When a merge happens before CI settles, check what
actually ran (`gh run view <id> --json jobs`) rather than trusting a green tick; and see
[[main-is-unprotected-auto-merge-does-not-wait]].
